```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE)
root<-if(dir.exists('results/summary'))'results/summary' else '.'
s<-readRDS(file.path(root,'summary.rds'));p<-s$performance
tab<-function(x,digits=3)knitr::kable(x,digits=digits,row.names=FALSE)
primary<-c('Conditional Wald','Full IF Wald','Full-system HC3 Wald','Delete-one Wald','Person percentile')
compact<-function(effect,methods=primary){
 x<-p[p$gamma==effect & p$method%in%methods,]
 x<-x[order(match(x$profile,s$profiles$profile),match(x$method,methods)),]
 x<-x[,c('profile','method','available','coverage','rejection','median_width','p95_width')]
 names(x)<-c('Profile','Method','Intervals / 100','Coverage','Zero exclusion','Median width','95th width percentile');x
}
```

## Purpose and interpretation

**The full-system correction improves coverage over plain IF in several weak-
information conditions, but at a substantial and sometimes extreme width cost.
It is not a general replacement for person bootstrap inference.** Actual
delete-one refits are much more widely available than the analytic methods,
yet their symmetric Wald intervals still under-cover in several profiles.

Key fresh findings:

- Full IF and HC3 each return **756/1,200** analyses. All 444 refusals are the
  pre-existing singular-measurement gate; there are no additional HC3 sensitivity
  refusals or driver/API errors. Delete-one returns **1,192/1,200**; person
  percentile returns **1,158/1,200**. These are paired structural analyses, not
  independent measurement-dataset counts.
- At truth .40, hard-profile HC3 coverage is **86.7–95.8%**, versus **71.1–85.9%**
  for plain IF on exactly the same 45–65 eligible datasets/profile. Paired gains
  are about 10–16 percentage points in low balanced, negative-correlation,
  small/short and unequal-information profiles; their unadjusted paired MC
  intervals exclude zero. Low larger-N gains only 3.1 points (MC interval includes
  zero). These are exploratory comparisons, not multiplicity-adjusted claims.
- On common HC3/bootstrap datasets, the median ratio of HC3 to bootstrap width
  is **1.62–1.85** in the hard profiles. HC3's 95th width percentiles are roughly
  **8.7–28.0**, versus **1.0–1.64** for bootstrap on their respective returned
  sets. No extreme intervals were capped or removed. Higher HC3 coverage often
  trades off detection and precision; mean SE alone obscures these tails.
- Delete-one effect coverage is **81.6–91.9%** in hard profiles, with 98–100
  returned intervals/profile. Person-percentile coverage is **81.5–96.9%**,
  with 92–98 intervals. The small/short point bias remains **−.178** at truth .40;
  none of the variance methods changes the original coefficient.
- Analytic deletion shifts closely match actual deletions in the high-reliability
  control (median focal relative RMSE **.012**). Among common hard-profile
  datasets with a singularity/floor/final-branch deletion transition, median
  relative RMSE ranges **.55–1.33**. Without those transitions it is about
  **.027–.201**. These selected-subset diagnostics are consistent with limitations
  of local deletion approximations; they do not isolate a causal mechanism.
- All six remote R-platform checks pass. Independent study validation checks
  all endpoints, actual centered/uncentered covariance formulas, public APIs,
  fresh inputs, source hashes and B prefixes. Half-step sensitivity changes no
  availability decisions and changes matched covariance by at most **4.86e-7**.

This study tests a specified full-system HC3-style correction and actual
whole-person delete-one refitting on **fresh random-number streams**. It is a
600-dataset exploratory validation screen: six profiles × 100 new measurement
datasets, each with paired null and nonzero structural outcomes. Its purpose
is to distinguish uncertainty propagation, leverage adjustment, refitting,
interval construction, bias and numerical availability. It does not select a
correction by maximizing observed coverage or claim uniform validity.

The numerical implementation and protocol were frozen before main results.
Earlier experiments remain unchanged. All methods retain the original REPAIR
point estimate; neither jackknife bias nor a simulation-estimated bias is
subtracted from the interval center.

## Data-generating design and fresh samples

```{r profiles}
tab(s$profiles)
```

The design retains the earlier noisy-predictor experiment: within-person time
is centered and sample-SD standardized; measurement
Y=.5*time+b0+b1*time+eps; random intercept/slope SDs .9 and correlation +/−.5;
Gaussian iid measurement errors calibrated to full-posterior slope reliability
.25 or .8. The unequal profile assigns half the people to 3 and half to 17
observations independently of latent effects/errors.

The structural outcome is Z=1.5+.4*b0+(gamma/.9)*b1+eta, with Var(Z)=1,
Gaussian homoskedastic eta and gamma=0/.40. Both recovered intercept and slope
enter as noisy predictors. All focal coefficients, SEs and endpoints are
multiplied by population SD .9. Gamma=0 is a null partial slope given the other
noisy random coefficient, not necessarily a null marginal association.

New L'Ecuyer-CMRG master seed **202610319** replaces the old 202610301; bootstrap
seed is 340000000+replication. Independent outer streams are paired across
profiles, and null/effect outcomes share measurement data/noise. This gives
1,200 structural analyses, not 1,200 independent measurement datasets. The
validation checks fresh input hashes against every old main-study input.

Main uses B499. The first three datasets/profile extend to B1999 and halve the
analytic derivative step; no subset was chosen by its results. Development
replication 801/B9 is excluded. No failed dataset is regenerated or replaced.

## What the methods estimate

**Conditional Wald** retains ordinary model-based M-MOM SEs. **Full IF Wald**
uses the existing complete influence-function sandwich, including measurement
estimation, structural weights/corrections and signed cross-stage covariance.
Both full-system methods use exact ML/REML measurement equations, with the global
REML fixed-design determinant retained. No ML scores at a REML fit are substituted.

**Full-system HC3 Wald** augments measurement parameters with unweighted observed/
error moments, weighted observed/error moments, log mean case weight and final
corrected coefficient equations. All preliminary coefficients, variance floors,
weights and correction multipliers are differentiated. Known error-free entries
remain fixed. The mean-weight equation normalizes the final coefficient equation,
cancelling an irrelevant common weight in OLS. That normalization was specified
during pre-main development after an OLS acceptance test detected a spurious
common-weight leverage effect.

For each person, solve the deleted augmented system's Jacobian at the original
parameters, using the exact deleted REML determinant. Sum **uncentered** outer
products of the resulting coefficient shifts. This recovers ordinary OLS HC3
in the matching special case. No measurement model is refitted. Original N and
policy/alpha remain fixed in this analytic structural correction. All deleted
systems and the original full influence must be usable; failures are never
silently replaced by HC0 or omitted. Sensitivities are centrally differentiated
with half-step, one-sided and active-branch checks and scaled conditioning gates.

This is an explicitly specified **HC3-style nonlinear-system candidate**;
leverage adjustments depend on the equation representation. It is not a derived
CR2/Satterthwaite procedure or a theorem of nominal finite-sample coverage.
The full derivation is in dev/leverage-jackknife-design.md in the PR. The OLS
anchor and augmented HC0/canonical IF identity check validate implementation,
not a general finite-sample approximation theorem.

**Delete-one Wald** refits each measurement and structural model on N-1 complete
people, updating all finite-N corrections and weights. Its variance is (N-1)/N
times the centered delete-one cross-product. Every complete coefficient vector
is required; a failed deletion invalidates inference. Singular but converged
native refits retain the existing replay policy and are recorded. Diagnostic
jackknife bias is not subtracted. The analytic and actual deletion methods
therefore differ in nonlinear re-estimation, finite-N updates, and HC3 versus
centered jackknife scaling.

**Person percentile** samples N complete people and fully refits measurement and
structural models, using the original complete-vector failure gate and type-7
percentile endpoints. **Bootstrap-SD Wald** instead uses the SD of those same
bootstrap coefficients in a normal symmetric interval; it is not a percentile-t
bootstrap. Frozen-measurement percentile and stage2 IF are diagnostic comparators.
The unequal profile additionally retains a count-preserving stratified comparator.
The earlier OLS-outcome stacked helper is not applied to this incompatible noisy-
predictor estimand; OLS HC3 is checked independently in package tests.

Normal reference intervals are primary. HC3 and delete-one t_(N−1) intervals
are prespecified secondary heuristics, not fitted effective degrees of freedom.
There is no data-selected multiplier or hidden finite-sample correction.

## Bias and the sampling-error distribution

```{r bias-figure, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'bias.png'))
```

All methods retain the same original coefficient, so separate method-specific
bias curves would duplicate the point estimator. This figure uses **all 100
fresh datasets per profile and truth**, showing each signed estimation error
and mean bias with its Monte Carlo uncertainty. It makes the negative bias in
the small/short and negative-correlation conditions visible alongside the
distribution's tails. The blue error bars concern the simulation mean bias;
they are not the confidence intervals whose coverage is assessed below.

Bias conditional on returning an interval can differ because eligibility
selects different datasets; those eligible-set summaries remain in performance.csv.

## Availability is part of the result

```{r availability, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'availability.png'))
```

```{r diagnostic-counts}
tab(as.data.frame(with(s$diagnostics,table(singular,full_if,leverage,delete_one))))
```

Analytic inference refuses singular/weakly identified original measurement fits
and unstable or weak deleted sensitivities. Actual refitting can remain usable
at singular native covariances; that difference is explicit, not an error hidden
by denominator changes. Every analytic refusal and native deletion failure is
archived. Coverage and zero exclusion below use **available intervals only**;
performance.csv also reports delivery-and-cover/detect per all 100 planned data.
Unavailable intervals remain NA, never valid non-rejections.

## Nonzero-effect coverage, detection and width

```{r coverage, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'coverage.png'))
```

```{r nonzero}
tab(compact(.4))
```

Zero exclusion here is detection, not type-I error. Median width can conceal
extreme intervals, so the 95th width percentile is also shown. All five methods
share original coefficients; the CSV retains overall and eligible bias/SD and
mean SEs rather than treating higher coverage alone as evidence of better inference.
Coverage figures display **50–100%**, rather than starting at zero, and retain
every plotted point and Monte Carlo bound. The dashed reference is 95%.

## Null-effect coverage and rejection

```{r null-coverage-figure, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'coverage_null.png'))
```

```{r null}
tab(compact(0))
```

At 100 planned datasets, a coverage near .95 has MC SE approximately .022.
Smaller eligible subsets have wider uncertainty. Figure bars and the CSV give
Wilson 95% Monte Carlo intervals; few-point changes do not establish superiority.

## Comparisons on common eligible datasets

```{r matched-coverage-figure, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'coverage_matched.png'))
```

This figure uses the **intersection of the five primary methods' eligibility**,
so each panel compares exactly the same datasets for every method. It is a
selected-cohort comparison, not population-wide calibration. Its rates can
differ from the method-specific returned-interval figures and from the pairwise
comparisons below, whose intersections are defined for each method pair.

```{r paired}
x<-s$paired[s$paired$gamma==.4 & s$paired$metric=='covers' &
 s$paired$method_a%in%c('Full-system HC3 Wald','Delete-one Wald'),]
tab(x[,c('profile','method_a','method_b','n','difference','mc_low','mc_high','a_only','b_only')])
```

Differences are method A minus method B. Bounds use paired per-dataset decision
differences and are exploratory, without multiplicity adjustment. No observed
discordance is not proof of equivalence; such bounds are not asserted. These
matched comparisons distinguish eligibility selection from interval construction.

## Secondary references and interval construction

```{r secondary}
tab(compact(.4,c('Full-system HC3 Wald','Full-system HC3 t','Delete-one Wald','Delete-one t',
                'Bootstrap-SD Wald','Person percentile')))
```

## Tail behavior: wide intervals and studentized errors

```{r width-tail-figure, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'width_tails.png'))
```

The width axis is logarithmic so typical intervals and extreme corrections
remain visible together. Circles show medians, diamonds empirical 95th
percentiles, and triangles the **largest observed intervals**. The full-system
HC3 tail is much longer in the difficult profiles; the typical-width summary
alone conceals that cost. Every returned interval contributes, and the maximum
is never dropped or winsorized. These are empirical summaries from 45–100
returned intervals per cell, not precise estimates of population-tail quantiles.

```{r width-exceedance-figure, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'width_exceedance.png'))
```

The step curves show the fraction of returned intervals wider than each
threshold, focusing vertically on the **upper 20% of widths**. All observed
thresholds remain on the logarithmic horizontal axis, and each curve reaches
zero at its observed maximum. The horizontal 5% line helps locate the upper
tail; finite-sample step locations need not equal interpolated type-7 quantiles
exactly. Eligibility still differs here; the denominators are those shown in
the method-specific coverage figures.

```{r studentized-tail-figure, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'studentized_tails.png'))
```

This diagnostic instead uses the same all-five-method eligibility cohort and
compares absolute errors divided by estimated SEs. The black dashed curve is
the standard-normal benchmark. At 1.96, a calibrated normal Wald procedure
would have about 5% exceedance; departures show that estimating a variance is
not enough to establish normal tail calibration. The upper 25% of this error
distribution is displayed, retaining all observed horizontal thresholds with
log(1+x) spacing. **Bootstrap SD is the symmetric Wald comparator**, not the
bootstrap percentile interval; a percentile interval cannot be diagnosed by
assuming its resample SD defines a symmetric normal interval.

## Branches, leverage and exact deletion

```{r branch-counts}
x<-s$branch_performance[s$branch_performance$gamma==.4 & s$branch_performance$method%in%primary,]
tab(x)
```

"Interior structural branch" means alpha:positive:alpha at a nonsingular original
measurement fit. "Active correction/floor" includes the other structural branches;
singular measurement fits have their own stratum. These are observational
diagnostic strata with different sample selection, not randomized causal contrasts.
Small strata are descriptive. Per-deletion floor/correction/singularity records
are retained separately in deletion_diagnostics.rds.

```{r deletion-switches}
x<-s$deletion_statistics
tab(aggregate(cbind(usable,singular_deletions,floor_switches,final_branch_switches)~profile+gamma,x,mean))
```

These counts refer to usable structural deletions (with their explicit counts)
and actual singular native refits. Final-branch changes distinguish the root
multiplier from the fixed-alpha multiplier using the declared minimum policy
and updated N-1; changes merely caused by alpha/(N-1) are not called branch
switches. Counts are descriptive and do not repair selection from failed fits.

Medians of available HC3 covariance contributions and ratios:

```{r components}
if(nrow(s$components))tab(aggregate(cbind(full,direct,measurement,cross,to_hc0)~profile,s$components,median))
```

The cross contribution is signed and need not increase the total variance.
Actual versus analytic deletion shifts on common available datasets:

```{r exact}
if(nrow(s$exact))tab(aggregate(cbind(relative_shift_rmse,focal_relative_shift_rmse,leverage_variance,jackknife_variance)~profile,
                             s$exact,median))
```

The relative RMSE divides the sum of squared analytic-minus-actual shifts by
the sum of squared actual shifts (with a small numerical floor). A discrepancy
can reflect curvature, branch changes, finite-N policy updates and centering/
scaling conventions; it is not automatically an implementation error. HC0
identity and OLS HC3 tests provide independent implementation anchors.

```{r exact-transition-strata}
if(nrow(s$exact)){
 x<-subset(s$exact,gamma==.4)
 x$deletion_transition<-x$singular_deletion | x$floor_switch | x$final_branch_switch
 a<-aggregate(focal_relative_shift_rmse~profile+deletion_transition,x,
              function(z)c(n=length(z),median=median(z)))
 tab(cbind(a[1:2],as.data.frame(a[[3]])))
}
```

The transition label indicates at least one actual deletion becoming singular
or changing floor/final-correction branch. These selected-subset comparisons
describe approximation behavior and do not establish causal effects of a branch.

## Prespecified sensitivity and independent validation

```{r steps}
tab(s$steps)
```

Availability changes under half steps and matched covariance differences are
reported without choosing the better-performing step. The B1999 subset retains
exact B499 prefixes; endpoint/availability changes are archived in
bootstrap_sensitivity.csv. This small tail subset is not a high-precision
coverage experiment.

All 78 fixed-subset percentile intervals were available at B499; **six become
unavailable at B1999** under the unchanged all-vector failure rule. Among the
72 returned at both B values, coverage classification is unchanged (all cover).
Median sums of absolute lower/upper endpoint changes are .0246 for person
percentile, .0310 frozen, and .0326 stratified. The sensitivity comparison
preserves those lost intervals; it does not silently condition the primary
analysis on successes or replace failures with new draws.

A **separate post hoc numerical audit**, motivated by the unusually wide tails,
checked the 12 largest HC3/HC0 variance ratios at h/2 and h/4. All 24 comparisons
remained available; the largest relative full-covariance change was **1.06e-4**
(about .011%). This supports treating the large corrections as properties of
the specified approximation rather than gross differencing error. It is not a
prespecified coverage comparison or proof of exact numerical precision. No
main estimate, step, threshold or interval was replaced. The rule and outputs
are retained in audit_extremes.R and posthoc_extreme_audit.csv.

The computational shortcut caches immutable individual OLS/design-inverse
ingredients for this iid matching-design DGP. **Every bootstrap and delete-one
measurement model is actually optimized**, with its fixed coefficients/sigma
and all structural equations updated. Eligibility requires full coefficient
vectors, not just a finite focal slope. Fixed subsets are verified against
24 complete public B99 bootstraps and 12 complete public jackknives. No failed
vector is replaced, trimmed or silently accepted.

```{r validation, results='asis'}
cat('```text\n',paste(readLines(file.path(root,'validation.txt')),collapse='\n'),'\n```\n',sep='')
```

## Reproducibility and limits

Numerical baseline is repair cbffe31, built on PR #21 head 6bb14dc. Subsequent
documentation and an explicit utils::tail qualification preserve the equations;
the frozen installed simulation library is not overwritten. The protocol,
drivers, source/library/reference hashes, sessions and full native histories
are retained in the research workspace's leverage_fresh directory. The PR's
dev/leverage-simulation bundle permits independent endpoint/rate verification
without fitting hundreds of thousands of models. Its README explains the
external research-source dependencies and distinguishes compact review evidence
from a complete raw optimization archive.

These results cover Gaussian iid measurement errors, six fixed reliability/
schedule conditions and a particular noisy-predictor structural design. They
do not validate informative missingness, misspecification, shared nuisance
effects, multiple measurement models or uniform boundary coverage. Neither a
finite interval nor an exact covariance decomposition establishes calibrated
inference; point bias, width, power and availability remain part of the assessment.

The package therefore retains both new methods as opt-in experimental tools.
The leverage result is useful for inspecting the complete system's sensitivity;
actual delete-one refits provide a complementary influence/branch diagnostic.
These results do not support making either symmetric interval the default
solution for weak noisy predictors. Bootstrap likewise remains imperfect,
especially with short panels and boundary/convergence issues.
